newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean defector may have spied for North - report.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean defector may have spied for North - report.

text.p: A South Korean religious leader who defected to communist North Korea last week might have been a spy while serving on a presidential advisory group, Seoul newspapers said on Monday.
South Korea's intelligence agency and police investigating the defection of Oh Ik-jae declined to comment on the newspaper reports.

Oh, 68, who turned up in Pyongyang on Friday, served on the Advisory Council on Democratic and Peaceful Unification, a presidential advisory body in South Korea. An official at the advisory body said Oh's term as adviser ended in June.
Oh was also a founding member of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics.

A senior police official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters he suspected Oh had maintained contacts with North Korean officials since 1993 when he met Pyongyang representatives of a religious group, Chondokyo, in Beijing.

Oh, who headed 130-year-old Chondokyo in the South until 1995, arrived in Pyongyang on Friday by train for "permanent residence", according to Pyongyang's official Korean Central News Agency's (KCNA).

"The authorities suspect Oh worked as a North Korean spy in the South for some time," said the influential Chosun Ilbo daily, which has had numerous scoops on North Korea-related issues in recent months.
Chosun Ilbo quoted an unidentified ruling camp official as saying that Oh appeared to have "left for America in March to escape the government's dragnet which was tightening towards him."
South Korea's state television broadcast North Korean TV footage showing Oh stepping out of a train at Pyongyang railway station.

In an arrival statement, he hailed North Korean leader Kim Jong-il as a hero and slammed the South Korean government for pursuing policies hampering the reunification of the Korean peninsula divided at the end of World War Two.

The police official said the North might also be using Oh in its propaganda to make up for the defection to the South earlier this year of Hwang Jang-yop, the highest-ranking Pyongyang official ever to flee his homeland.
Hwang, a top ideologue who arrived in Seoul in April via China and the Philippines, has said there are North Korean moles among high-ranking Seoul officials.
Seoul newspaper editorials criticised the government for not being able to stop the defection.
"If Oh defected after realising that he was being investigated, then there seems to be a large hole in our security system," the Dong-a Ilbo newspaper said in an editorial.
"Through a thorough investigation of pro-North Koreans, such incidents must be prevented in the future."
A Chosun Ilbo editorial said: "This society provides an environment for such pro-North Koreans to survive."
The two Koreas have been locked in Cold War confrontation since the 1950-53 Korean war.
